title: Problem Overview and Imports
content: **Problem Overview.** Erdős Problem #702 (the Erdős-Sós conjecture on singleton intersections): For k ≥ 4, if F is a k-uniform family over {1,...,n} with |F| > C(n-2, k-2), must F contain two sets A, B with |A ∩ B| = 1? Answer: YES (Frankl 1977). The bound is tight. Imports Finset basics and SimpleGraph.
mathContext: This problem belongs to **extremal set theory**, which asks: how large can a set family be while avoiding a particular configuration? Here the forbidden configuration is a 'singleton intersection' — two sets sharing exactly one element. The extremal family (all k-sets containing two fixed elements) achieves C(n-2, k-2) sets while avoiding singleton intersections, since any two sets in this family share at least {x, y}. Frankl proved this construction is optimal: any larger family must contain a singleton pair. The condition k ≥ 4 is necessary — the theorem fails for k = 3.

title: Set Families: Ground Set and k-Uniformity
content: **groundSet, IsKUniform, IsOverGroundSet.** The ground set {1,...,n} is defined via `Finset.range` with a shift. IsKUniform requires all sets in F to have cardinality exactly k. IsOverGroundSet requires all sets to be subsets of {1,...,n}.
mathContext: The k-uniformity constraint (all sets have the same size) is the standard setting for extremal set theory problems. Without uniformity, the problem trivializes: a non-uniform family can contain sets of different sizes whose intersection structure is unconstrained. The ground set formalization uses `Finset.range n |>.map ⟨(· + 1), ...⟩` to produce {1, 2, ..., n} rather than {0, 1, ..., n-1}, matching the standard mathematical convention. In hypergraph language, F is a k-uniform hypergraph on vertex set [n].

title: Intersection Patterns
content: **SingletonIntersection, AvoidsSingletonIntersections, HasSingletonPair.** A singleton intersection means |A ∩ B| = 1 (exactly one common element). A family avoids singleton intersections if no distinct pair achieves this. HasSingletonPair is the existential: some distinct pair in F shares exactly one element.
mathContext: The singleton intersection condition |A ∩ B| = 1 is the simplest non-trivial intersection constraint beyond 'disjoint' (|A ∩ B| = 0) and 'intersecting' (|A ∩ B| ≥ 1). For k-sets containing two fixed points x, y, any intersection has size ≥ 2, so singleton intersections are automatically avoided. The predicate AvoidsSingletonIntersections is a universal quantifier over all distinct pairs, making it hard to maintain as the family grows — this is the essence of Frankl's theorem. The problem is a special case of the general **r-intersection avoidance** problem studied in Problem #703.

title: Extremal Construction
content: **extremal_construction.** Fix two elements x, y ∈ {1,...,n}. The family of all k-sets containing both x and y has exactly C(n-2, k-2) members (choose k-2 elements from the remaining n-2). This family avoids singleton intersections because any two sets share at least {x, y}, giving |A ∩ B| ≥ 2.
mathContext: This extremal construction is a **sunflower with 2-element kernel**: all sets in the family share the common core {x, y}, and the 'petals' (the remaining k-2 elements) can be anything. The size C(n-2, k-2) counts the number of ways to choose petals. The construction is tight — Frankl's theorem shows no larger family can avoid singleton intersections. The fact that the extremal family has such a simple structure (all sets through two fixed points) is characteristic of many extremal set theory results, where optimal constructions are often 'trivial' in structure.

title: Frankl's Theorem and Katona's Case
content: **frankl_theorem and katona_k4.** Frankl (1977) proved the Erdős-Sós conjecture for all k ≥ 4: if |F| > C(n-2, k-2) for a k-uniform family F over {1,...,n}, then F contains a singleton intersection pair. Katona had previously proved the k = 4 case (unpublished).
mathContext: Frankl's proof uses the **shifting technique** (also called compression): replacing elements in sets to make the family 'left-shifted' without creating new singleton intersections. After shifting, the family has a simpler structure that can be analyzed combinatorially. The key insight is that shifting preserves the avoidance property while concentrating the family on low-numbered elements, eventually forcing a contradiction with the size bound. Katona's earlier proof for k = 4 used a more direct counting argument. The axiomatization in Lean records both results as trusted facts, with the main theorem `erdos_702` derived directly from `frankl_theorem`.

title: Special Cases and k = 3 Failure
content: **k = 4 example and k = 3 failure.** For k = 4, n = 6: the bound is C(4, 2) = 6, verified by `native_decide`. For k = 3, the theorem fails: there exist 3-uniform families exceeding C(n-2, 1) = n-2 that still avoid singleton intersections.
mathContext: The failure for k = 3 is significant and reveals a structural boundary. For 3-element sets, it is possible to construct large families where every pair of sets either shares 0 or 2 elements (completely disjoint or sharing an edge). The **Steiner triple system** and related designs provide such constructions. Specifically, the Fano plane (7 points, 7 lines, each line a 3-set) has the property that any two lines meet in exactly 1 point — but its complement (the non-lines) can avoid singleton intersections. The condition k ≥ 4 ensures enough 'room' in each set that the shifting argument works.

title: Proof Technique and Related Problems
content: **Shifting method and connection to #703.** Frankl's proof uses the shifting (compression) technique from extremal set theory. Problem #703 generalizes to r-intersection avoidance in non-uniform families, solved by Frankl-Rödl (1987).
mathContext: The **shifting technique** is one of the most powerful tools in extremal set theory. Given a family F, a shift replaces occurrences of element j by element i (for i < j) whenever the result is not already in F. This operation preserves or decreases intersection sizes, so if the original family avoids singleton intersections, so does the shifted family. After applying all shifts, the family is 'left-shifted' (closed under replacing larger elements with smaller ones), which imposes strong structural constraints. Problem #703 extends to general (non-uniform) families: Frankl and Rödl proved T(n, r) ∼ n/r for the maximum family size avoiding r-intersections, winning a $250 prize from Erdős.

title: Main Theorem: erdos_702
content: **erdos_702.** The main theorem restates Frankl's result: for k ≥ 4, any k-uniform family over {1,...,n} with more than C(n-2, k-2) sets contains a singleton intersection pair. Defined as `erdos_702 := frankl_theorem`. Status: SOLVED.
mathContext: The theorem `erdos_702` is a direct application of `frankl_theorem`, demonstrating the clean axiomatization approach: deep results from published papers are recorded as axioms, and the main problem statement is derived as a consequence. The formalization also includes string-valued metadata (`erdos_702_answer`, `erdos_702_status`) and `#check` commands for verification. The result places Problem #702 among the fully resolved Erdős problems, alongside #703 (also Frankl) and #644 (partially resolved by EFKT92).
